A_target.statement:
Let $A, B$ be [[Definition:Formal Language|languages]] over an [[Definition:Alphabet|alphabet]] $\Sigma$.
Then the [[Definition:Smallest Element|least]] solution of the equation:
:$X = A X \cup B$
is:
:$X = A^* B$
If $\epsilon \notin A$, this solution is [[Definition:Unique|unique]].

B_source.statement:
Let $F$ be a [[Definition:Increasing Mapping|monotone]] operator on the [[Definition:Power Set|power set]] $\powerset S$ that preserves unions of increasing chains.
Then $F$ has a [[Definition:Least Fixed Point|least fixed point]]:
:$\displaystyle \mu F = \bigcup_{n \mathop \ge 0} \map {F^n} \O$

substitutions.the monotone operator: the map sending a language X to the prefix concatenated with X, united with the base
substitutions.the iteration from the empty object: successive approximations accumulating longer prefixes of the star
substitutions.the least fixed point: the star of the prefix concatenated with the base

derived.the limit of the iteration: the union over all repetition counts of the prefix applied to the base
derived.uniqueness of the solution: guaranteed only when the prefix does not contain the empty word

validity_conditions: The operator is monotone in the unknown language, so iterating it from the empty set gives an increasing chain whose union is the least fixed point.
The nth iterate consists of words formed by at most n copies of the prefix followed by the base, so the union is exactly the star of the prefix times the base.
If the prefix contains the empty word the equation has many solutions and only the least is given by the formula, so uniqueness requires excluding that case.
proof_plan:
Define $\map F X = A X \cup B$ on the [[Definition:Power Set|power set]] $\powerset {\Sigma^*}$.
[[Definition:Concatenation of Languages|Concatenation]] and [[Definition:Set Union|union]] are [[Definition:Increasing Mapping|monotone]], so $F$ is monotone.
The equation states that $X$ is a [[Definition:Fixed Point|fixed point]] of $F$.

Hence:
:$\displaystyle \mu F = \bigcup_{k \mathop \ge 0} A^k B = A^* B$
which is the [[Definition:Least Fixed Point|least fixed point]] by the source result.

Suppose $\epsilon \notin A$ and $X$ is any solution.
A word $w \in X$ of length $m$ unwinds in at most $m$ steps, so $X \subseteq A^* B$.
Hence the solution is [[Definition:Unique|unique]].
If $\epsilon \in A$, then $A^* \paren {B \cup C}$ is also a solution for every language $C$, so uniqueness fails.
{{qed}}
